propositions.text: Whether the trial judge erred in concluding Crown’s repudiation of plea agreement was abuse of process breaching s.7 Charter rights.
propositions.quote: The question on this appeal is whether the trial judge erred in concluding that the Crown’s repudiation of a plea agreement was an abuse of process in breach of the appellant’s rights under s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms .

propositions.text: Courts below were divided on the appropriate standard to measure repudiation conduct.
propositions.quote: More specifically, the courts below were divided on the appropriate standard against which to measure the repudiation conduct.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the issue is whether the trial judge erred on Crown repudiation of plea agreement as abuse of process breaching s.7 Charter rights, and courts below disagreed on the standard.

propositions.text: Application judge held repudiation of plea agreement is conduct subject to usual criminal trial court control.
propositions.quote: The application judge held that the repudiation of a plea agreement is a matter of conduct or tactics which is subject to the usual control of the criminal trial court

propositions.text: Repudiation by Assistant Deputy Minister was not justified as Crown counsel’s decision was reasonably defensible.
propositions.quote: In the case at bar, the repudiation of the plea agreement by the Assistant Deputy Minister of the Criminal Justice Division was not justified, as Crown counsel’s decision to enter into a plea agreement was “reasonably defensible”.

propositions.text: Repudiation was abuse of process breaching accused’s s.7 security and liberty interests; Crown directed to honour agreement.
propositions.quote: Thus, he concluded that the repudiation of the plea agreement was an abuse of process in breach of the accused’s s. 7 security and liberty interests and directed the Crown to honour the agreement.

propositions.text: Appellant pleaded guilty to lesser offence and was acquitted on more serious charges.
propositions.quote: The appellant subsequently pleaded guilty to a lesser offence and was acquitted on the more serious charges.

paragraphs.summary: The application judge found repudiation was unjustified abuse of process breaching s.7 rights and ordered Crown to honour agreement; appellant pleaded guilty to lesser offence and was acquitted.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal overturned application judge, holding repudiation is prosecutorial discretion reviewable only for abuse of process.
propositions.quote: The Alberta Court of Appeal overturned the application judge’s decision, holding that the repudiation of a plea agreement is a matter of prosecutorial discretion, reviewable only for abuse of process

propositions.text: Application judge erred testing Crown counsel’s decision against “reasonably defensible” standard; should review repudiation circumstances.
propositions.quote: It held that the application judge erred in testing Crown counsel’s decision against a “reasonably defensible” standard. Rather, he should have reviewed the circumstances surrounding the subsequent decision to repudiate.

propositions.text: Abuse of process under s.7 requires conduct causing prejudice rendering trial unfair or affecting justice system integrity.
propositions.quote: The relevant inquiry for abuse of process under s. 7 of the Charter is whether there is conduct which either causes prejudice to the accused by rendering the trial unfair, or affects the integrity of the justice system itself.

propositions.text: Absent prejudice, proof of prosecutorial misconduct, improper motive or bad faith is required to find abuse of process.
propositions.quote: In the absence of prejudice which renders the trial unfair, there must be proof of “prosecutorial misconduct, improper motive or bad faith in the approach, circumstances or ultimate decision to repudiate”

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found no evidence of abuse of process and ordered new trial, setting aside application judge’s order, plea and acquittals.
propositions.quote: Applying this test, the Court of Appeal found no evidence to support a finding of abuse of process in the circumstances of this case. The application judge’s order, the resulting plea and the acquittals were set aside, and a new trial was ordered.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal held repudiation is prosecutorial discretion reviewable only for abuse of process, found no abuse, set aside plea and acquittals, ordered new trial.

propositions.text: Appellant Olga Maria Nixon appeals to this Court.
propositions.quote: The appellant, Olga Maria Nixon, appeals to this Court.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant Olga Maria Nixon appeals to this Court.

propositions.text: Agrees with Court of Appeal that application judge applied incorrect test for abuse of process.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I agree with the Court of Appeal that the application judge applied the incorrect test for abuse of process.

propositions.text: Agrees no basis to find appellant’s s.7 rights breached; would dismiss appeal.
propositions.quote: I also agree that there is no basis for finding that the appellant’s s. 7 rights were breached in the circumstances of this case. I would dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The Court agrees with Court of Appeal that application judge used wrong test and finds no breach of s.7 rights; would dismiss appeal.

propositions.text: Appellant charged with Criminal Code offences including dangerous driving causing death and bodily harm, and impaired driving.
propositions.quote: The appellant, Ms. Nixon, was charged with several Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 , offences, including dangerous driving causing death, dangerous driving causing bodily harm, and parallel charges for impaired driving.

propositions.text: Charges arose from motor vehicle accident on September 2, 2006, killing a husband and wife and injuring their son.
propositions.quote: The charges arose as a result of a motor vehicle accident which occurred on September 2, 2006. The Crown alleged that Ms. Nixon drove her motor home through an intersection without stopping and struck another vehicle, killing a husband and wife and injuring their young son.

propositions.text: Roadside screening and breath samples showed high blood alcohol levels; expert extrapolated 225-250 mg/100 mL at accident time.
propositions.quote: A roadside screening test was administered at the scene, followed by breath samples which resulted in readings of 200 mg of alcohol in 100 mL of blood. Expert extrapolation concluded that Ms. Nixon’s blood alcohol level would have been between 225 and 250 mg per 100 mL at the time of the accident.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states appellant was charged with dangerous driving and impaired driving after a fatal accident with high blood alcohol levels.

propositions.text: Appellant elected trial by judge and jury; preliminary inquiry held March 1, 2007.
propositions.quote: Given that Ms. Nixon elected trial by judge and jury, the matter proceeded to a preliminary inquiry on March 1, 2007.

propositions.text: Crown counsel had concerns about evidence admissibility and probative value, did not adduce breath sample results at preliminary hearing but reserved right for trial.
propositions.quote: Crown counsel who had carriage of the case at the time had concerns about some of the evidence, in particular the admissibility of the breathalyzer results and the probative value of the eyewitness evidence that a motor home had been seen driving erratically some time before the accident. Based on his assessment, Crown counsel did not adduce the breath sample results at the preliminary hearing, although he specifically reserved the right to call this evidence at trial.

propositions.text: Crown informed judge it would not seek committal on charges other than dangerous driving; appellant consented to committal on dangerous driving.
propositions.quote: He also informed the presiding judge that the Crown would not be seeking a committal on any charge other than the dangerous driving counts. Ms. Nixon consented to a committal order on the dangerous driving charges.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant elected trial by jury; Crown counsel had evidence concerns, did not adduce breath results at preliminary, reserved for trial; Crown limited committal to dangerous driving, appellant consented.

propositions.text: In May 2007, counsel discussed plea to careless driving with joint sentence recommendation of $1,800 fine.
propositions.quote: Following the preliminary inquiry, additional discussions were held between counsel during the first weeks of May 2007 regarding a plea to a charge of careless driving under the Traffic Safety Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. T-6, with a joint sentence recommendation for a $1,800 fine.

propositions.text: Written agreement entered May 22; appellant re-elected mode of trial anticipating guilty plea June 5.
propositions.quote: Counsel ultimately entered into a written agreement to that effect on May 22, and Ms. Nixon re-elected her mode of trial in anticipation of entering a guilty plea to the lesser charge on June 5.

paragraphs.summary: Counsel agreed on plea to careless driving with $1,800 fine; written agreement entered May 22; appellant re-elected trial mode expecting guilty plea June 5.

propositions.text: Crown counsel discussed plea with colleagues and supervisor who reluctantly agreed; report prepared for senior officials.
propositions.quote: Before making the offer for a plea resolution, Crown counsel had discussed the matter in general terms with some of his colleagues in the Crown’s office, including his immediate supervisor who reluctantly agreed with the terms of the proposed agreement. Due to the sensitive nature of the case, a report was also prepared for senior officials in the justice department.

propositions.text: Acting ADM saw report and proposed resolution, became concerned, initiated inquiry, prompting adjournment from June 5 to June 26; defence not informed of reason.
propositions.quote: When the Acting Assistant Deputy Minister (“ADM”) of the Criminal Justice Division of the office of the Attorney General saw the report and the proposed resolution scheduled to be perfected a few days later, he became concerned and initiated an inquiry. This in turn prompted an adjournment of the June 5 date to June 26. The defence was not informed of the reason for the adjournment at the time.

paragraphs.summary: Crown counsel discussed plea with colleagues; Acting ADM became concerned after seeing report, initiated inquiry, adjourned plea date without informing defence.

propositions.text: ADM obtained legal opinions, concluded Crown counsel’s assessment was flawed for ignoring total evidence.
propositions.quote: The ADM obtained additional legal opinions about the merits of the Nixon prosecution and about the repudiation of plea agreements. Based on the results of this research, the ADM concluded that Crown counsel’s assessment of the strength of the case was flawed as he had failed to consider the totality of the evidence.

propositions.text: ADM concluded plea to careless driving was contrary to interests of justice and would bring administration of justice into disrepute.
propositions.quote: In his view, a plea to careless driving in the circumstances was contrary to the interests of justice and would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.

propositions.text: ADM concluded appellant could be restored without prejudice to prior position before plea agreement.
propositions.quote: The ADM also concluded that Ms. Nixon could be restored without prejudice to the position she had been in prior to entering into the plea agreement.

propositions.text: Decision to not proceed on impaired driving counts maintained; ADM instructed Crown counsel to withdraw plea agreement and proceed to trial on dangerous driving.
propositions.quote: Thus, it was resolved that the decision by Crown counsel at the preliminary hearing not to proceed on the impaired driving counts would be maintained. However, the ADM instructed Crown counsel to withdraw the May 22 resolution agreement and to proceed to trial on the dangerous driving charges in accordance with the committal order.

paragraphs.summary: ADM obtained opinions, found Crown counsel’s assessment flawed, repudiated plea agreement, maintained impaired driving counts dropped, ordered trial on dangerous driving.

propositions.text: Appellant brought s.7 Charter application alleging abuse of process, seeking court order to complete plea agreement.
propositions.quote: In response to this turn of events, Ms. Nixon brought an application under s. 7 of the Charter , alleging abuse of process and seeking a court direction requiring the Crown to complete the agreement.

propositions.text: Application judge began inquiry, reserved judgment, noted Attorney General’s ultimate power to conduct prosecutions as affirmed in Krieger.
propositions.quote: Ayotte Prov. Ct. J. of the Provincial Court of Alberta embarked on an inquiry into the matter, at the conclusion of which he reserved judgment. At the outset of his written reasons, the application judge noted that the Attorney General has the ultimate power to initiate, conduct and terminate prosecutions, as affirmed by this Court in Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, 2002 SCC 65, [2002] 3 S.C.R. 372.

propositions.text: Courts rarely interfere with prosecutorial discretion but when discretion exercised in favour of proceeding, matter becomes subject to court processes.
propositions.quote: He also acknowledged that the courts will rarely interfere with the exercise of prosecutorial discretion. In his view, however, “when that discretion is exercised in favour of proceeding, the matter becomes subject to the processes and procedures sanctioned by the court” (para. 12).

propositions.text: Negotiations after charges laid are matters of tactics or conduct subject to court review.
propositions.quote: Thus, he held that negotiations between counsel after charges are laid were matters of tactics or conduct which were subject to review by the court.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant applied under s.7 alleging abuse of process; application judge noted Attorney General’s prosecutorial power, rare court interference, but found post-charge negotiations subject to court review.

propositions.text: Application judge concluded Crown’s ability to repudiate plea agreement akin to trial judge rejecting joint sentence submission; test is whether plea agreement is reasonably defensible.
propositions.quote: He concluded that the Crown’s ability to repudiate a plea agreement is akin to the discretion of a trial judge to reject a joint submission on sentence: the determinative test was whether the plea agreement was “reasonably defensible”.

propositions.text: Application judge found no evidence of political interference or bad faith in ADM’s repudiation decision.
propositions.quote: After reviewing the relevant evidence, he concluded that “there is absolutely no evidence” of political interference (para. 22) and “nothing to suggest that [the ADM’s] action was taken in bad faith or to accommodate a real or perceived political stance of his Minister of Justice” (para. 25).

paragraphs.summary: Application judge held repudiation test is whether plea agreement is reasonably defensible and found no political interference or bad faith in ADM’s decision.

propositions.text: Application judge emphasized test is whether plea agreement was reasonably defensible, not just different conclusions by others.
propositions.quote: The application judge emphasized that the relevant test is whether the plea agreement was “reasonably defensible”. In his view, if the Crown is to justify its course of action to repudiate the agreement, then it must do more than establish that others would have reached a different conclusion.

propositions.text: Repudiation not justified as Crown counsel’s assessment was reasonably defensible.
propositions.quote: In the case at bar, he concluded that the repudiation of the plea agreement was not justified, as Crown counsel’s assessment of the case was “reasonably defensible”.

propositions.text: If original bargain not contrary to public interest or justice administration, prejudice to accused irrelevant; if required, prejudice found here.
propositions.quote: The application judge held further that where the court is satisfied that the original bargain, if honoured, would not be contrary to the public interest and would not bring the administration of justice into disrepute, it is irrelevant whether the accused suffered prejudice. He added that if he were required to find prejudice, he would do so here.

propositions.text: Appellant prejudiced because defence led to believe breath sample evidence would not be adduced, so did not explore at preliminary hearing.
propositions.quote: In his view, Ms. Nixon was prejudiced because defence counsel was led to believe that the evidence of breath samples would not be adduced at trial and, consequently, did not explore that issue at the preliminary hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Application judge found repudiation unjustified as plea was reasonably defensible; prejudice irrelevant if bargain not contrary to public interest; found prejudice here due to defence assumptions.

propositions.text: Application judge concluded appellant’s s.7 right to security of person breached; directed Crown to proceed with agreement before another judge.
propositions.quote: The application judge concluded that Ms. Nixon’s s. 7 right to security of the person was breached and, by way of remedy, he directed the Crown to proceed with the agreement before another judge.

propositions.text: Appellant pleaded guilty to careless driving, sentenced to $1,800 fine, acquitted of Criminal Code offences.
propositions.quote: Ms. Nixon subsequently pleaded guilty to the offence of careless driving, was sentenced to a fine of $1,800, and was acquitted of the Criminal Code offences.

paragraphs.summary: Application judge found s.7 breach, ordered Crown to honour agreement; appellant pleaded guilty to careless driving, fined, acquitted of other offences.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal allowed Crown appeal, holding application judge erred in finding s.7 Charter rights violated.
propositions.quote: The Crown appealed the acquittals. The Court of Appeal of Alberta allowed the appeal, holding that the application judge erred in law by finding that Ms. Nixon’s s. 7 Charter rights were violated.

propositions.text: Application judge used wrong test to distinguish prosecutorial discretion from prosecutor’s tactics and conduct before court.
propositions.quote: Paperny J.A. (Côté and Slatter JJ.A. concurring) found that the application judge used the wrong test to distinguish between matters that fall within the scope of prosecutorial discretion and those more properly characterized as a prosecutor’s tactics and conduct before the court.

propositions.text: Relevant inquiry is whether decision falls within core prosecutorial discretion: whether prosecution should be brought, continued or ceased, and for what.
propositions.quote: Paperny J.A. stated: “Rather, the relevant inquiry is whether the impugned decision falls within the core of the prosecutor’s discretion: is it a decision as to whether a prosecution should be brought, continued or ceased, and if so, what it should be for?”

propositions.text: Decision to continue prosecution is prosecutorial discretion not reviewable by courts except for abuse of process.
propositions.quote: Here, the decision to continue the prosecution is a matter of prosecutorial discretion which is not reviewable by the courts, subject to the doctrine of abuse of process.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal allowed Crown appeal, found application judge erred using wrong test, held decision to continue prosecution is prosecutorial discretion reviewable only for abuse of process.

propositions.text: Application judge erred in requiring plea agreement repudiation only if original decision unreasonable or not reasonably defensible.
propositions.quote: Paperny J.A. held that the application judge further erred in finding that a plea agreement can only be repudiated if the original decision is unreasonable or not “reasonably defensible”.

propositions.text: Review should focus on circumstances of ADM’s repudiation decision to determine abuse of process.
propositions.quote: Instead of reviewing the initial decision of Crown counsel, he should have reviewed the circumstances surrounding the ADM’s decision to repudiate the plea agreement to determine whether that decision amounted to an abuse of process.

propositions.text: Under s.7, abuse of process requires conduct causing prejudice rendering trial unfair or affecting justice system integrity.
propositions.quote: The relevant inquiry under s. 7 of the Charter is whether there is conduct which either causes prejudice to the accused by rendering the trial unfair, or affects the integrity of the justice system itself.

propositions.text: Due deference to Crown’s constitutional role requires deferential standard of review.
propositions.quote: As she put it, “Due regard to the constitutional role occupied by the Crown demands a deferential standard of review”

propositions.text: No evidence supported abuse of process finding; acquittals set aside; new trial ordered on dangerous driving charges.
propositions.quote: Applying this test, Paperny J.A. concluded that there was no evidence to support a finding of abuse of process in the circumstances of this case. The acquittals were set aside and a new trial was ordered on the dangerous driving charges.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal held application judge erred in test, review should focus on ADM’s repudiation circumstances for abuse of process; no abuse found; acquittals set aside; new trial ordered.

propositions.text: Ms. Nixon appeals to this Court.
propositions.quote: Ms. Nixon appeals to this Court.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Nixon appeals to this Court.

propositions.text: Parties debated whether repudiation is prosecutorial discretion reviewable only for abuse of process or tactics/conduct before court subject to court control.
propositions.quote: Much of the debate between the parties in this Court was centred on whether the Crown’s repudiation of a plea agreement is a matter of “prosecutorial discretion” reviewable only for abuse of process, or a matter of “tactics or conduct before the court” governed by the inherent jurisdiction of the criminal trial court to control its own process.

propositions.text: The distinction’s importance was fully canvassed and explained in Krieger.
propositions.quote: The crucial importance of this distinction was fully canvassed and explained in Krieger.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes parties debated if repudiation is prosecutorial discretion or court-controlled tactics; Krieger fully canvassed this distinction.

propositions.text: In Krieger, Law Society claimed jurisdiction over all lawyers including Attorney General’s Crown counsel.
propositions.quote: In Krieger, the Law Society of Alberta claimed that it had jurisdiction over all members of the profession within the province, including those employed by the Attorney General of Alberta.

propositions.text: Law Society sought to investigate bad faith or dishonesty allegation against Crown counsel for failure to disclose evidence.
propositions.quote: Thus, it purported to investigate an allegation of bad faith or dishonesty against Crown counsel in connection with a failure to disclose relevant information to the accused as required by law.

propositions.text: Attorney General and Krieger challenged Law Society’s jurisdiction, arguing prosecutorial discretion decisions are immune from review.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General and Krieger, who was Crown counsel, challenged the Law Society’s jurisdiction, arguing that decisions made by an agent of the Attorney General in the conduct of a prosecution were immune from review under the doctrine of prosecutorial discretion.

paragraphs.summary: Krieger involved Law Society claiming jurisdiction over Crown counsel; Law Society investigated bad faith; Attorney General and Krieger challenged jurisdiction as prosecutorial discretion immune from review.

propositions.text: Court affirmed Attorney General’s office independence as constitutional principle in Canada.
propositions.quote: Iacobucci and Major JJ., writing for the Court, reviewed the nature and development of the Attorney General’s office in Canada and affirmed the independence of the office as “a constitutional principle in this country” (para. 30).

propositions.text: Attorney General must act independently of partisan concerns in prosecutorial decisions; courts will not interfere with executive authority in prosecutorial decision-making.
propositions.quote: The Court explained that the principle of independence requires that the Attorney General “act independently of partisan concerns when supervising prosecutorial decisions” and how it “finds further form in the principle that courts will not interfere with his exercise of executive authority, as reflected in the prosecutorial decision‑making process” (paras. 30 and 31).

propositions.text: Independence of Attorney General is fundamental to rule of law; courts cannot supervise prosecutorial decision-making except for abuse of process.
propositions.quote: The Court stressed the fundamental importance of the principle of independence in these terms (at para 32): The court’s acknowledgment of the Attorney General’s independence from judicial review in the sphere of prosecutorial discretion has its strongest source in the fundamental principle of the rule of law under our Constitution. Subject to the abuse of process doctrine, supervising one litigant’s decision-making process — rather than the conduct of litigants before the court — is beyond the legitimate reach of the court. . . . The quasi-judicial function of the Attorney General cannot be subjected to interference from parties who are not as competent to consider the various factors involved in making a decision to prosecute. To subject such decisions to political interference, or to judicial supervision, could erode the integrity of our system of prosecution. Clearly drawn constitutional lines are necessary in areas subject to such grave potential conflict. [Emphasis added.]

paragraphs.summary: Krieger affirmed Attorney General’s constitutional independence, requiring partisan independence and no court interference in prosecutorial decisions except abuse of process.

propositions.text: Law Society retained jurisdiction over Krieger's alleged misconduct as outside prosecutorial discretion doctrine
propositions.quote: The Court ultimately concluded, however, that the Law Society retained jurisdiction over Krieger’s alleged misconduct, as it was a matter that fell outside the scope of the doctrine.

propositions.text: Distinction between prosecutorial discretion and tactics/conduct is central to this appeal
propositions.quote: In explaining the proper contours of prosecutorial discretion, the Court drew the distinction between acts of prosecutorial discretion, and tactics or conduct.

propositions.text: Prosecutorial discretion involves core powers protected by independence principle
propositions.quote: “Prosecutorial discretion” is a term of art. It does not simply refer to any discretionary decision made by a Crown prosecutor. Prosecutorial discretion refers to the use of those powers that constitute the core of the Attorney General’s office and which are protected from the influence of improper political and other vitiating factors by the principle of independence.

propositions.text: Core elements of prosecutorial discretion include bringing prosecution, stays, plea acceptance, withdrawal, control of private prosecution
propositions.quote: Without being exhaustive, we believe the core elements of prosecutorial discretion encompass the following: (a) the discretion whether to bring the prosecution of a charge laid by police; (b) the discretion to enter a stay of proceedings in either a private or public prosecution, as codified in the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 579 and 579.1 ; (c) the discretion to accept a guilty plea to a lesser charge; (d) the discretion to withdraw from criminal proceedings altogether: R. v. Osborne (1975), 25 C.C.C. (2d) 405 (N.B.C.A.); and (e) the discretion to take control of a private prosecution: R. v. Osiowy (1989), 50 C.C.C. (3d) 189 (Sask. C.A.).

propositions.text: Prosecutorial discretion concerns ultimate decisions on prosecution nature, extent, and participation
propositions.quote: Significantly, what is common to the various elements of prosecutorial discretion is that they involve the ultimate decisions as to whether a prosecution should be brought, continued or ceased, and what the prosecution ought to be for.

propositions.text: Decisions on tactics or conduct before court are not prosecutorial discretion but court's inherent jurisdiction
propositions.quote: Decisions that do not go to the nature and extent of the prosecution, i.e., the decisions that govern a Crown prosecutor’s tactics or conduct before the court, do not fall within the scope of prosecutorial discretion. Rather, such decisions are governed by the inherent jurisdiction of the court to control its own processes once the Attorney General has elected to enter into that forum.

paragraphs.summary: The Court found Law Society jurisdiction over Krieger's misconduct outside prosecutorial discretion, explaining prosecutorial discretion's core elements and distinguishing it from tactics.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal erred in treating Crown's repudiation of plea agreement as core prosecutorial discretion
propositions.quote: Ms. Nixon submits that the Court of Appeal erred when it concluded that the Crown’s decision to renege on its agreement with the defence was an aspect of its traditional, constitutionally protected, core discretionary powers.

propositions.text: Repudiation of plea agreement is a reversal in tactic subject to broader review
propositions.quote: She contends that the Crown’s decision to resile from the agreement constitutes a reversal in tactic subject to broader review.

propositions.text: Plea agreement is akin to contract; Crown should be held to its word absent vitiating flaws
propositions.quote: Given that Crown counsel’s offer had been accepted by the defence, the resulting plea agreement is akin to a contractual undertaking. A bargain is a bargain, it is argued. Absent some vitiating flaw in the negotiating process, such as mistake, misrepresentation or fraud, the Crown should be held strictly to its word.

propositions.text: No need to show prejudice or bad faith; repudiation alone is abuse of process unless it disreputes justice
propositions.quote: It is not necessary for the applicant to show that she has been prejudiced, or to establish independent acts of “bad faith” or “flagrant impropriety”. Unless the Crown can satisfy the court that implementing the plea agreement would itself bring the administration of justice into disrepute, the repudiation of a valid plea agreement, in and of itself, constitutes an abuse of process.

propositions.text: Application judge adopted correct approach; Court should restore his decision
propositions.quote: In short, Ms. Nixon argues that the application judge adopted the correct approach and urges the Court to restore his decision.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Nixon argues the Court of Appeal erred treating plea repudiation as core discretion; she urges strict enforcement of plea agreements absent flaws.

propositions.text: CTLA supports that Crown's plea agreement promise is a lawyer's undertaking to be strictly fulfilled
propositions.quote: The intervener Criminal Trial Lawyers’ Association (“CTLA”) supports Ms. Nixon’s argument that the Crown’s promise to enter into a plea agreement is an undertaking “like any other given by a lawyer”. It argues that the undertaking “must be strictly and scrupulously fulfilled” and that an abuse of process need not be shown before the agreement may be summarily enforced by a court

paragraphs.summary: CTLA supports Ms. Nixon, arguing plea agreement promises must be strictly fulfilled and enforceable without showing abuse of process.

propositions.text: CLA supports Ms. Nixon that plea repudiation is not core prosecutorial discretion and warrants judicial review
propositions.quote: The Criminal Lawyers’ Association (Ontario) (“CLA”) also supports Ms. Nixon’s position that the repudiation of a plea agreement does not fall within “core” Crown discretion identified in Krieger. Thus, the CLA submits that judicial review of a repudiation decision is warranted even in the absence of “flagrant impropriety” or bad faith.

propositions.text: Test for repudiation should mirror sentencing judge's rejection test: would it bring justice into disrepute?
propositions.quote: Rather, the test for allowing Crown repudiation of a plea agreement should be essentially the same as the test applied for allowing a sentencing judge to reject a joint submission: would the proposed resolution bring the administration of justice into disrepute?

propositions.text: Repudiation is abuse of process unless Crown shows agreement would disrepute justice and accused restored
propositions.quote: The CLA submits that “[r]epudiation is an abuse of process unless the Crown discharges its onus of demonstrating that the contemplated agreement would have brought the administration of justice into disrepute and the accused can be restored to his or her initial position”

paragraphs.summary: CLA supports Ms. Nixon, arguing plea repudiation is abuse of process unless Crown proves agreement disreputes justice and accused restored.

propositions.text: Respondent says plea agreement and repudiation are core prosecutorial discretion acts, reviewable only for abuse of process
propositions.quote: the respondent, the Attorney General of Alberta, takes the position that both the plea agreement and the repudiation are acts that fall within the scope of the doctrine of prosecutorial discretion. As such, neither is open to review or supervision by the courts, except through an allegation of abuse of process.

propositions.text: Test for abuse of process requires bad faith or flagrant impropriety for core prosecutorial discretion
propositions.quote: Abuse of process that involves core prosecutorial discretion requires proof of bad faith or flagrant impropriety by the Crown.

propositions.text: No evidence of bad faith or prejudice; Ms. Nixon restored to pre-plea position
propositions.quote: Here, there was no evidence of any such conduct by the Crown officials in their review and repudiation of the plea agreement. Nor did Ms. Nixon suffer any prejudice as a result of the repudiation, given that she was restored to the position she was in at the conclusion of the preliminary inquiry, before the plea agreement was struck.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal rightly found no breach of s. 7 rights
propositions.quote: Therefore, the Court of Appeal rightly concluded that there was no basis for finding a breach of her s. 7 rights.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues plea agreement and repudiation are core prosecutorial discretion, requiring bad faith for abuse; no bad faith or prejudice here.

propositions.text: Three Attorneys General support respondent, arguing application judge's approach conflicts with prosecutorial independence in Krieger
propositions.quote: Attorneys General from three provinces intervened in support of the respondent’s position. In particular, they submit that the approach adopted by the application judge runs afoul with the principle of independence affirmed in Krieger.

propositions.text: Attorney General of Ontario says Krieger was misinterpreted; all prosecutorial discretion immune except for abuse of process
propositions.quote: The Attorney General of Ontario submits that this Court’s decision in Krieger has been misinterpreted by lower courts. It asks this Court to confirm that Krieger was never intended to narrow the area of protected prosecutorial discretion, or to create a schism in threshold tests for finding an abuse of process depending on whether a decision is considered “core” or “non-core”. All acts of prosecutorial discretion are immune from judicial supervision, subject only to the same high threshold for abuse of process.

paragraphs.summary: Three Attorneys General support respondent, arguing application judge's approach conflicts with prosecutorial independence and misinterprets Krieger.

propositions.text: AGBC stresses trial courts should only review prosecutorial discretion after threshold determination and evidentiary record
propositions.quote: the Attorney General of British Columbia (“AGBC”) emphasizes the importance of criminal trial courts not proceeding with a review of prosecutorial discretion in the absence of a “threshold determination” that the inquiry is warranted. In the absence of evidence of irremediable impairment to the fair trial interests of the accused, a criminal trial court should only proceed with an application for relief challenging prosecutorial discretion under the residual category of abuse of process if there is an evidentiary record capable of supporting the claim.

propositions.text: Trial judge erred by fully examining reasons for plea repudiation without evidence of improper motive or bad faith
propositions.quote: This approach helps to avoid scenarios such as the case at bar, where the trial judge engaged in a full examination of the reasons behind the decision to renege on the plea agreement, even though there was nothing to suggest that the decision was motivated by improper considerations, or was made in bad faith.

paragraphs.summary: AGBC argues trial courts should only review prosecutorial discretion after threshold and evidence; trial judge erred by full examination without bad faith evidence.

propositions.text: AGM stresses Attorney General's supervisory role and that bona fide repudiation decisions are proper institutional checks
propositions.quote: the Attorney General of Manitoba (“AGM”) intervenes to underscore the importance of the Attorney General’s supervisory role over the exercise of prosecutorial discretion. Acknowledging that the repudiation of plea agreements is and should be rare, it argues that “when the Attorney General, or a senior delegate, makes a bona fide decision to overturn a plea agreement that he or she determines is contrary to the public interest, that decision is part of the proper and usual institutional checks and balances necessary for the justice system to function properly”

paragraphs.summary: AGM emphasizes Attorney General's supervisory role and that bona fide repudiation decisions are proper institutional checks and balances.

propositions.text: No dispute that Crown's plea offer is core prosecutorial discretion under Krieger
propositions.quote: None of the participants in this appeal disputes that Crown counsel’s decision to resolve the proceedings by accepting a plea to a lesser offence falls within the scope of prosecutorial discretion as defined in Krieger.

propositions.text: Application judge's line at 'discretion exercised in favour of proceeding' cannot be sustained
propositions.quote: To the extent that the application judge’s analysis suggests that anything occurring after the charges are laid falls outside the scope of prosecutorial discretion, it cannot be sustained.

propositions.text: Drawing line at courtroom door neuters prosecutorial discretion's purpose to resolve cases by plea or discontinuance
propositions.quote: As noted by Paperny J.A., to artificially draw the line at the courtroom door “effectively neuters some of the primary purposes of prosecutorial discretion, to resolve cases by accepting pleas to lesser charges and to discontinue prosecutions”

paragraphs.summary: Court finds plea offer is core prosecutorial discretion; application judge's line excluding post-charge discretion is unsustainable and neuters prosecutorial purpose.

propositions.text: ADM's decision to repudiate plea agreement is core prosecutorial discretion
propositions.quote: Applying this test, she held that the ADM’s decision to repudiate the plea agreement “fell squarely within the core elements of prosecutorial discretion” (para. 33). I agree.

propositions.text: ADM decided prosecution should continue for dangerous driving, not careless driving
propositions.quote: The ADM effectively decided that the prosecution against Ms. Nixon should be continued and that it should be for the Criminal Code offences of dangerous driving, not for the traffic infraction of careless driving.

propositions.text: Prosecutorial discretion continues throughout proceedings; not spent at initiation or plea agreement
propositions.quote: Prosecutorial discretion was not spent with the decision to initiate the proceedings, nor did it terminate with the plea agreement. So long as the proceedings are ongoing, the Crown may be required to make further decisions about whether the prosecution should be continued and, if so, in respect of what charges.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees ADM's repudiation of plea is core prosecutorial discretion continuing throughout proceedings, not ending at plea agreement.

propositions.text: Crown's decision to resile from plea agreement is subject only to abuse of process review under Krieger
propositions.quote: Thus, it follows that the Crown’s ultimate decision to resile from the plea agreement and to continue the prosecution is subject to the principles set out in Krieger: it is only subject to judicial review for abuse of process.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes Crown's repudiation of plea agreement is subject only to abuse of process review per Krieger.

propositions.text: How initial plea offer exercise of prosecutorial discretion affects abuse of process analysis is difficult question
propositions.quote: The more difficult question in this appeal is how the initial exercise of prosecutorial discretion — Crown counsel’s offer to resolve the matter on the basis of a plea to a lesser charge — should figure in the analysis regarding abuse of process.

propositions.text: Will review parties' divergent views and then review abuse of process law
propositions.quote: Before dealing with these arguments, I will review the law on abuse of process.

paragraphs.summary: Court identifies difficult issue of how plea offer affects abuse of process analysis and plans to review parties' views and abuse of process law.

propositions.text: Before Jewitt, uncertainty existed whether courts could stay proceedings for abuse of process or only Attorney General could under Criminal Code
propositions.quote: Until this Court’s decision in R. v. Jewitt, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 128, there was much controversy about whether a court had the power to stay validly instituted criminal proceedings for abuse of process.

propositions.text: Superior courts had inherent jurisdiction to stay abusive proceedings
propositions.quote: The inherent jurisdiction of a superior court to control its own process by staying abusive proceedings had long been recognized in Canada.

propositions.text: Uncertainty whether criminal courts had discretion to stay for abuse or if power reserved to Attorney General under s. 508 (now s. 579)
propositions.quote: However, it remained uncertain whether criminal courts had the discretion to stay proceedings for abuse of process, or whether this was a power reserved for the Attorney General under s. 508 (now s. 579 ) of the Criminal Code (pp. 131-32).

paragraphs.summary: Court explains pre-Jewitt uncertainty about courts' power to stay proceedings for abuse of process versus Attorney General's power under Criminal Code.

propositions.text: Jewitt recognized trial court residual discretion to stay proceedings for abuse of process in narrow circumstances
propositions.quote: Jewitt put an end to the uncertainty by recognizing that a trial court judge had a “residual discretion” to stay proceedings to remedy abuse of process.

propositions.text: Abuse of process applies where trial would violate fundamental justice or be oppressive or vexatious
propositions.quote: The Court held that the common law doctrine could be applied in narrow circumstances “where compelling an accused to stand trial would violate those fundamental principles of justice which underlie the community’s sense of fair play and decency and to prevent the abuse of a court’s process through oppressive or vexatious proceedings” (pp. 136-37).

paragraphs.summary: Jewitt recognized trial courts' residual discretion to stay proceedings for abuse of process where trial violates fundamental justice or is oppressive.

propositions.text: Common law abuse of process distinct from Charter due to focus on judicial integrity and different burdens of proof
propositions.quote: Initially, the common law doctrine of abuse of process was viewed as analytically distinct from Charter considerations since its focus was more on maintaining confidence in the integrity of the judicial system than on protecting individual rights.

propositions.text: Common law abuse of process required 'clearest of cases' burden; Charter violation required balance of probabilities
propositions.quote: For an applicant to establish a violation under the Charter , the burden of proof was the balance of probabilities standard. For an applicant to successfully invoke the court’s common law power to stay proceedings for abuse of process, the burden of proof was the more onerous “clearest of cases” standard.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes common law abuse of process was distinct from Charter with higher burden of proof for stays than Charter violations.

propositions.text: O’Connor merged common law and Charter abuse of process under s.7, recognizing overlap in protecting fairness and judicial integrity
propositions.quote: Ten years later in R. v. O’Connor, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 411, the Court noted that there was much overlap between the Charter and the common law doctrine of abuse of process, as the latter had found application in circumstances involving state conduct touching upon both “the integrity of the judicial system and the fairness of the individual accused’s trial” (para. 73).

propositions.text: Different Charter guarantees may apply depending on abuse of process circumstances
propositions.quote: Depending on the circumstances, different Charter guarantees may be engaged by the alleged abuse of process and thus some claims may be better addressed by reference to the specific procedural guarantee.

propositions.text: Two categories of abuse of process under s.7: prosecutorial conduct affecting trial fairness and conduct undermining judicial integrity
propositions.quote: The Court identified two categories of abuse of process which would be caught by s. 7 of the Charter : (1) prosecutorial conduct affecting the fairness of the trial; and (2) prosecutorial conduct that “contravenes fundamental notions of justice and thus undermines the integrity of the judicial process” (para. 73).

paragraphs.summary: O’Connor merged common law and Charter abuse of process under s.7, identifying two categories: affecting trial fairness and undermining judicial integrity.

propositions.text: No practical utility in maintaining separate common law and Charter abuse of process regimes due to burdens and remedies
propositions.quote: The Court held further that there was no practical utility in maintaining two distinct analytic regimes based on the different burdens of proof.

propositions.text: Charter s.24(1) allows remedies less drastic than stay; abuse of process balancing remains essential
propositions.quote: The Court made clear, however, that the fusion of common law and Charter claims of abuse of process under s. 7 of the Charter does not alter “the essential balancing character of abuse of process”.

propositions.text: Charter gives judges a 'scalpel' to fashion remedies balancing fairness, societal interests, and judicial integrity
propositions.quote: I see no reason why such balancing cannot be performed equally, if not more, effectively under the Charter , both in terms of defining violations and in terms of selecting the appropriate remedy to perceived violations.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains fusion of common law and Charter abuse of process claims under s.7, emphasizing balancing and flexible remedies under Charter.

propositions.text: Abuse of process requires harm of sufficient degree to justify stay; lesser harms do not suffice
propositions.quote: while s. 24(1) of the Charter allows for a wide range of remedies, this does not mean that abuse of process can be made out by demonstrating a lesser degree of harm, either to the accused’s fair trial interests or to the integrity of the justice system.

propositions.text: Balancing societal and individual concerns defines abuse of process's essential character
propositions.quote: Achieving the appropriate balance between societal and individual concerns defines the essential character of abuse of process.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds abuse of process requires significant harm balancing societal and individual interests to justify stay of proceedings.

propositions.text: First abuse category concerns trial fairness; prejudice key; prosecutorial misconduct not prerequisite
propositions.quote: Under the first category of cases, the concern is about the fairness of the accused’s trial. Establishing prejudice of the requisite degree is key to meeting the test; proof of prosecutorial misconduct, while relevant, is not a prerequisite: R. v. Keyowski, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 657.

paragraphs.summary: First abuse of process category concerns trial fairness; prejudice is key, misconduct not required, per Keyowski.

propositions.text: Test for abuse is whether compelling trial violates justice principles or is oppressive/vexatious; misconduct not required
propositions.quote: The Court reiterated that the test for abuse of process was whether “compelling an accused to stand trial would violate those fundamental principles of justice which underlie the community’s sense of fair play and decency”, or where the proceedings are “oppressive or vexatious” (pp. 658-59, quoting from Jewitt, at pp. 136-37).

propositions.text: Misconduct or improper motive not required to find abuse; many factors considered
propositions.quote: To define “oppressive” as requiring misconduct or an improper motive would, in my view, unduly restrict the operation of the doctrine.

paragraphs.summary: Test for abuse is whether trial violates justice principles or is oppressive; misconduct not required; many factors considered.

propositions.text: Prejudice to the accused is relevant but not determinative under the residual abuse of process category.
propositions.quote: Under the residual category of cases, prejudice to the accused’s interests, although relevant, is not determinative.

propositions.text: Prejudice here is an act undermining society’s expectations of fairness in justice administration.
propositions.quote: prejudice under the residual category of cases is better conceptualized as an act tending to undermine society’s expectations of fairness in the administration of justice.

propositions.text: L’Heureux-Dubé J. in R. v. Conway explained abuse of process as unfair treatment that tarnishes court integrity.
propositions.quote: Under the doctrine of abuse of process, the unfair or oppressive treatment of an appellant disentitles the Crown to carry on with the prosecution of the charge... to allow it to proceed would tarnish the integrity of the court.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains prejudice is relevant but not determinative in abuse of process, citing R. v. Conway on fairness and court integrity.

propositions.text: Test for stay of proceedings for abuse of process requires prejudice perpetuated by trial and no other remedy available.
propositions.quote: A stay of proceedings will only be appropriate when: “(1) the prejudice caused by the abuse in question will be manifested, perpetuated or aggravated through the conduct of the trial, or by its outcome; and (2) no other remedy is reasonably capable of removing that prejudice”

paragraphs.summary: The court states the test for stay of proceedings for abuse of process requires prejudice perpetuated by trial and no other remedy.

propositions.text: Before applying abuse of process framework, court will address arguments on plea agreement's impact.
propositions.quote: Before applying this framework of analysis to this case, I will address some of the arguments advanced in this appeal on how the plea agreement should impact the analysis of abuse of process.

paragraphs.summary: The court will first address arguments on how plea agreements affect abuse of process analysis.

propositions.text: Plea agreement should be regarded as a contractual undertaking and enforced like lawyers’ undertakings.
propositions.quote: it is argued that a plea agreement should be regarded as a contractual undertaking and enforced just as any other lawyers’ undertaking.

propositions.text: This argument fails because plea agreements have a public dimension and differ from usual lawyers’ undertakings.
propositions.quote: This argument cannot be sustained. It completely ignores the public dimension of a plea agreement.

propositions.text: Law Society of Alberta states plea agreements are not usual lawyers’ undertakings due to policy considerations.
propositions.quote: the Law Society of Alberta specifically recognizes in the comment to Rule 27 of its Code of Professional Conduct that “[a]n agreement between the prosecution and defence regarding the plea to be entered is not considered a usual lawyers’ undertaking due to the policy considerations involved”

propositions.text: Vitiating factors like mistake or fraud do not fully capture public interest in repudiating plea agreements.
propositions.quote: Vitiating factors, such as mistake, misrepresentation or fraud, which usually inform a private party’s right to resile from a bargain, do not fully capture the public interest considerations which are at play in any decision to repudiate a plea agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues plea agreements are contractual undertakings, but the court finds this fails due to public interest and Law Society rules.

propositions.text: Plea agreements should be summarily enforced like lawyers’ undertakings and repudiation alone warrants remedy.
propositions.quote: A plea agreement cannot be summarily enforced by the court as any other lawyers’ undertaking, as Ms. Nixon contends. It is also wrong to suggest that repudiation, in and of itself, warrants a judicial remedy even in the absence of prejudice

propositions.text: This argument wrongly assumes repudiation is outside prosecutorial discretion and not subject to constitutional principles.
propositions.quote: This argument is founded on the erroneous premise that the decision to repudiate a plea agreement falls outside the scope of prosecutorial discretion and, as such, is not subject to the constitutional principles set out in Krieger.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues plea agreements must be enforced and repudiation alone warrants remedy, but the court rejects this as ignoring prosecutorial discretion.

propositions.text: Lawyers’ undertaking analogy highlights importance of honouring plea agreements but does not fully apply.
propositions.quote: to the extent that the lawyers’ undertaking analogy underscores the importance of honouring plea agreements, it can usefully contribute to the analysis.

propositions.text: Martin Committee Report found resolution agreements are undertakings reflecting counsel’s duties of integrity and responsibility.
propositions.quote: the Committee found resolution agreements in criminal proceedings to be “in the nature of undertakings”. The duty of counsel to honour resolution agreements was regarded as “a particular example of the duties of integrity and responsibility”

propositions.text: Honouring resolution agreements is ethically imperative and practically necessary to resolve most criminal court issues.
propositions.quote: Honouring resolution agreements was not only “ethically imperative”, but also a “practical necessity”, as these agreements “dispose of the great bulk of the contentious issues that come before the criminal courts in Ontario”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the lawyers’ undertaking analogy highlights plea agreement importance, citing the Martin Committee Report on counsel’s duties.

propositions.text: Binding effect of plea agreements is vital to justice administration and helps resolve most criminal cases fairly and efficiently.
propositions.quote: the binding effect of plea agreements is a matter of utmost importance to the administration of justice. It goes without saying that plea resolutions help to resolve the vast majority of criminal cases in Canada

paragraphs.summary: The court states plea agreements are vital to justice and resolve most criminal cases fairly and efficiently.

propositions.text: Disagreements among Crown counsel on plea agreements are unsurprising but Crown must often accept initial decisions to maintain confidence.
propositions.quote: there may be instances where different Crown counsel will invariably disagree about the appropriate plea agreement in a particular case... the Crown may simply have to live with the initial decision that has been made.

propositions.text: If defence cannot rely on plea agreements, benefits for accused and justice system are lost; repudiation must be rare.
propositions.quote: if agreements arrived at over the course of resolution discussions cannot be relied upon by the accused, the benefits that resolutions produce for both the accused and the administration of justice cannot be achieved... the situations in which the Crown can properly repudiate a resolution agreement are, and must remain, very rare.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Crown counsel disagreements are expected but repudiation must be rare to preserve plea agreement benefits.

propositions.text: All Attorneys General agree plea agreements should be repudiated only in exceptional, rare circumstances.
propositions.quote: All Attorneys General who have participated in this appeal agree that a plea agreement should only be repudiated in exceptional and rare circumstances.

propositions.text: Lawyers’ undertaking analogy cannot determine standard for repudiation; Crown’s duty to system integrity prevails if values clash.
propositions.quote: While the sanctity of agreements entered into is an important principle... Crown counsel’s primary duty is to the integrity of the system. Accordingly, in the rare cases where these two values clash, the latter must prevail.

propositions.text: Argument that plea agreements are simply contractual undertakings must fail.
propositions.quote: As a result, the argument that a plea agreement can simply be characterized as a contractual undertaking must fail.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds plea agreements should rarely be repudiated; lawyers’ undertaking analogy fails as Crown’s duty to system integrity prevails.

propositions.text: Applicant and application judge urged court to apply 'reasonably defensible test' like trial judge rejecting joint sentence submissions.
propositions.quote: This Court was also urged, as was the application judge, “to equate the ability of the Attorney General to resile from a plea agreement to the ability of a trial judge to reject a joint submission on sentence

propositions.text: Crown initially advanced this argument but later withdrew it.
propositions.quote: The Crown advanced this argument in first instance but subsequently resiled from this position.

propositions.text: Application judge adopted 'reasonably defensible test' and found plea agreement was reasonably defensible, concluding repudiation was abuse of process.
propositions.quote: the application judge crafted the “reasonably defensible test”... Having determined that it was, ... the application judge concluded that the repudiation of the plea agreement amounted to an abuse of process.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant and judge urged 'reasonably defensible test'; Crown withdrew; judge found plea agreement defensible and repudiation abusive.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal held application judge erred by reversing onus and asking wrong question about plea agreement repudiation.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal held that the application judge erred in multiple ways by adopting this approach... his “selected framework for analysis caused him to ask the wrong question”.

propositions.text: Court agrees with Court of Appeal that review should focus on repudiation circumstances, not initial plea agreement decision.
propositions.quote: he should have reviewed the circumstances surrounding the repudiation to determine whether that decision amounted to an abuse of process

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with Court of Appeal that application judge erred by focusing on plea agreement defensibility, not repudiation circumstances.

propositions.text: Application judge’s reasonableness review of prosecutorial discretion conflicts with Krieger principles.
propositions.quote: The application judge’s assessment of a decision made in the exercise of prosecutorial discretion for “reasonableness” runs contrary to the principles set out in Krieger.

propositions.text: Courts must not second-guess prosecutorial discretion to maintain independence and impartiality.
propositions.quote: By straying into the arena and second-guessing the decision, the reviewing court effectively becomes a supervising prosecutor and risks losing its independence and impartiality.

propositions.text: Krieger holds prosecutorial discretion decisions are beyond legitimate court review absent misconduct or bad faith.
propositions.quote: Due regard to the constitutionally separate role of the Attorney General... puts such decisions “beyond the legitimate reach of the court” (Krieger, at para. 32).

propositions.text: Court only looks behind prosecutorial decisions for misconduct, improper motive or bad faith in repudiation.
propositions.quote: it only looks behind the decision for “proof of the requisite prosecutorial misconduct, improper motive or bad faith in the approach, circumstances or ultimate decision to repudiate”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds application judge erred by reviewing prosecutorial discretion for reasonableness, contrary to Krieger principles.

propositions.text: Analogy to trial judge rejecting joint sentence submissions is unhelpful for measuring repudiation conduct.
propositions.quote: the analogy to the trial judge’s rejection of a joint submission on sentencing is not particularly helpful in determining the standard against which to measure the repudiation conduct.

propositions.text: Sentencing judge’s role differs qualitatively from prosecutorial decision to resile from plea agreement.
propositions.quote: The sentencing judge who is faced with a joint submission is engaged in a qualitatively different process than the prosecutorial authority faced with the decision of whether or not to resile from a plea agreement.

propositions.text: Sentencing judge imposes fit sentence based on evidence and agreed facts from plea negotiations.
propositions.quote: The role of the sentencing judge is to impose a fit sentence... When the accused pleads guilty, the circumstances... are generally determined on the basis of agreed facts.

propositions.text: Prosecutor must consider all circumstances including public interest when deciding to honour or resile from plea agreement.
propositions.quote: the prosecuting authority who is faced with the decision whether to honour or to resile from a plea agreement must consider the entirety of circumstances, including the public interest

propositions.text: Sentencing principles on joint submissions cannot be transposed to prosecutorial repudiation decisions.
propositions.quote: sentencing principles relating to joint submissions cannot usefully be transposed in this context.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds sentencing judge analogy unhelpful because prosecutorial repudiation involves broader public interest considerations.

propositions.text: Court will now apply abuse of process doctrine to this case.
propositions.quote: I now turn to the circumstances of this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court proceeds to apply abuse of process doctrine to the case.

propositions.text: Ms. Nixon’s abuse of process claim does not appear based on prejudice to fair trial interests.
propositions.quote: Ms. Nixon’s claim of abuse of process does not appear to be grounded in an alleged prejudice to her fair trial interests.

propositions.text: Ms. Nixon alleges prejudice in various ways unrelated to trial fairness.
propositions.quote: She certainly alleges that she was prejudiced in various ways by the course of events, but most of the alleged prejudice has nothing to do with trial fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Ms. Nixon’s abuse of process claim is not grounded in prejudice to fair trial interests, though she alleges other prejudice.

propositions.text: Ms. Nixon describes emotional and psychological trauma and increased anxiety from Crown’s change of position.
propositions.quote: she describes in an affidavit the emotional and psychological trauma she suffered... and then explains how she suffered increased anxiety as a result of the Crown’s change of position.

propositions.text: Court accepts Ms. Nixon was affected but finds no bearing on trial fairness.
propositions.quote: There is no reason to doubt that Ms. Nixon was affected by the course of events as she describes in her affidavit. However, this has no bearing on the fairness of her trial.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Nixon alleges emotional trauma from Crown’s change, but the court finds no impact on trial fairness.

propositions.text: Ms. Nixon relies on application judge’s finding that counsel was misled about breath sample evidence at preliminary hearing.
propositions.quote: Ms. Nixon relies on the application judge’s finding that she was prejudiced because her counsel was led to believe that the evidence of breath samples would not be adduced at trial

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found this finding was a palpable and overriding error; Crown reserved right to call evidence at trial.
propositions.quote: this finding constitutes a palpable and overriding error, as Crown counsel at the preliminary hearing specifically reserved the right to call the evidence at trial.

propositions.text: Crown is not obliged to present all evidence at preliminary hearing; evidence can be tested at trial.
propositions.quote: there is no obligation on the Crown to present all of its evidence at the preliminary hearing and the evidence can still be tested at trial

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Nixon alleges counsel was misled about evidence, but court finds this was error and Crown reserved right to call evidence.

propositions.text: Ms. Nixon argues repudiation compromises her right to silence and defence, affecting choice of counsel.
propositions.quote: “the giving up of her right to silence would seriously compromise and diminish her defence... perhaps ultimately affecting her right to her choice of counsel”

propositions.text: Court finds no merit; repudiation occurred before plea; Court of Appeal set aside plea and order; effect on defence is speculative.
propositions.quote: I see no merit to this argument. The plea agreement was repudiated before Ms. Nixon entered her plea... the alleged effect on her counsel’s ability to defend her is entirely speculative.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Nixon argues repudiation harms defence and counsel choice, but court finds no merit and notes plea was repudiated before plea entered.

propositions.text: Whether repudiation of plea agreement amounts to abuse of process under residual category balancing fairness and system integrity.
propositions.quote: Did the repudiation of the plea agreement, based on all of the circumstances, amount to an abuse of process?

propositions.text: Was Crown’s repudiation conduct unfair, oppressive, or tainted by bad faith to tarnish judicial system integrity?
propositions.quote: was the Crown’s repudiation conduct so unfair or oppressive to Ms. Nixon, or so tainted by bad faith or improper motive, that to allow the Crown to now proceed... would tarnish the integrity of the judicial system?

paragraphs.summary: The court poses the issue whether the Crown’s repudiation was abusive enough to tarnish judicial integrity.

propositions.text: AGBC argues courts should not review prosecutorial discretion without threshold determination that inquiry is warranted.
propositions.quote: AGBC intervened... to emphasize the importance of criminal trial courts not proceeding with a review of prosecutorial discretion in the absence of a “threshold determination” that the inquiry is warranted.

propositions.text: Court agrees threshold inquiry is needed but finds evidence of plea agreement and repudiation meets threshold.
propositions.quote: I agree that a court should not embark on an inquiry into the reasons behind an act of prosecutorial discretion without a proper evidentiary foundation. However, it is my view that evidence that a plea agreement has been entered into and subsequently reneged by the Crown meets the requisite threshold.

paragraphs.summary: AGBC argues for threshold before reviewing prosecutorial discretion; court agrees but finds plea agreement repudiation meets threshold.

propositions.text: Mandating a preliminary determination on the utility of a Charter-based inquiry is not new and is supported by R. v. Pires.
propositions.quote: As the AGBC rightly points out, mandating a preliminary determination on the utility of a Charter -based inquiry is not new: R. v. Pires, 2005 SCC 66, [2005] 3 S.C.R. 343.

propositions.text: Trial judges must control proceedings and can decline evidentiary hearings without reasonable likelihood of assistance.
propositions.quote: For our justice system to operate, trial judges must have some ability to control the course of proceedings before them. One such mechanism is the power to decline to embark upon an evidentiary hearing at the request of one of the parties when that party is unable to show a reasonable likelihood that the hearing can assist in determining the issues before the court.

propositions.text: Threshold requirements in criminal law may be imposed for pragmatic reasons and are not anomalies.
propositions.quote: Similar thresholds are also imposed in other areas of the criminal law, they are not an anomaly. Threshold requirements may be imposed for pragmatic reasons alone.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues preliminary Charter inquiry thresholds are established; the court states trial judges can control proceedings and impose pragmatic thresholds.

propositions.text: A threshold burden is required for abuse of process claims against prosecutorial discretion, not bare allegations.
propositions.quote: Given that such decisions are generally beyond the reach of the court, it is not sufficient to launch an inquiry for an applicant to make a bare allegation of abuse of process.

propositions.text: An example of insufficient abuse of process allegation is differing Crown decisions on charges against co-accused without more evidence.
propositions.quote: For example, it would not suffice for an applicant to allege abuse of process based on the fact that the Crown decided to pursue the charges against him but withdrew similar charges against a co-accused.

propositions.text: Without more evidence, courts cannot look behind prosecutorial discretion exercises.
propositions.quote: Without more, there would be no basis for the court to look behind the exercise of prosecutorial discretion.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds abuse of process claims require more than bare allegations; mere differing prosecutorial decisions are insufficient.

propositions.text: Repudiation of a plea agreement is evidence the Crown reneged and is crucial to fair criminal justice administration.
propositions.quote: However, the repudiation of a plea agreement is not just a bare allegation. It is evidence that the Crown has gone back on its word. As everyone agrees, it is of crucial importance to the proper and fair administration of criminal justice that plea agreements be honoured.

propositions.text: Repudiation of a plea agreement provides the evidentiary threshold to review prosecutorial discretion for abuse of process.
propositions.quote: evidence that a plea agreement was entered into with the Crown, and subsequently reneged by the Crown, provides the requisite evidentiary threshold to embark on a review of the decision for abuse of process.

propositions.text: The evidentiary burden shifts to the Crown to explain reasons for repudiation once evidence of repudiation is shown.
propositions.quote: the evidentiary burden shifts to the Crown to enlighten the court on the circumstances and reasons behind its decision to resile from the agreement.

propositions.text: The ultimate burden of proving abuse of process remains on the applicant, with a stringent test.
propositions.quote: The ultimate burden of proving abuse of process remains on the applicant and, as discussed earlier, the test is a stringent one.

propositions.text: If the Crown provides little or no explanation, this favors the applicant in proving abuse of process.
propositions.quote: if the Crown provides little or no explanation to the court, this factor should weigh heavily in favour of the applicant in successfully making out an abuse of process claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds repudiation of plea agreements meets the threshold for abuse of process review, shifting evidentiary burden to the Crown.

propositions.text: Prosecutorial discretion acts are subject to judicial review for abuse of process, including repudiation of plea agreements.
propositions.quote: Acts of prosecutorial discretion are not immune from judicial review. Rather, they are subject to judicial review for abuse of process.

propositions.text: Repudiation may constitute abuse of process if it causes trial unfairness or undermines judicial integrity.
propositions.quote: Depending on the circumstances, the repudiation of a plea agreement may well constitute an abuse of process, either because it results in trial unfairness or meets the narrow residual category of abuse that undermines the integrity of the judicial process.

propositions.text: The Krieger standard applies to repudiation, emphasizing the importance of honouring resolution agreements.
propositions.quote: In applying the Krieger standard to the repudiation of plea agreements, the principles set out in these reasons, notably at paras. 46-48, on the importance of honouring resolution agreements must be kept in mind.

propositions.text: Examples of abuse include arbitrary repudiation without inquiry or systemic overruling of plea agreements by Crown counsel.
propositions.quote: Consider, for example, if the repudiation was made arbitrarily, without inquiry into the circumstances leading to the plea agreement, and without regard to any resulting prejudice to the accused. Alternatively, consider if there was evidence of a systemic problem in a particular jurisdiction where Crown counsel regularly and summarily overruled the preceding Crown counsel’s exercise of discretion whenever they disagreed with the terms of the agreed upon plea resolution.

propositions.text: An application judge may find bad faith or flagrant impropriety sufficient to constitute abuse of process in such circumstances.
propositions.quote: In my view, an application judge may well be persuaded in such circumstances that the Crown acted in bad faith or with flagrant impropriety to a degree sufficient to constitute an abuse of process.

paragraphs.summary: The court states prosecutorial discretion, including repudiation, is reviewable for abuse of process under Krieger, with examples of bad faith abuse.

propositions.text: A threshold showing is required before judicial review of prosecutorial discretion; evidence of repudiation meets this threshold.
propositions.quote: Thus, it is my view that a threshold showing must be made before the court embarks on a judicial review of an exercise of prosecutorial discretion. Evidence of repudiation meets that threshold.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds evidence of repudiation meets the threshold for judicial review of prosecutorial discretion.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal correctly found no evidence supporting abuse of process in this case.
propositions.quote: In this case, I agree with the Court of Appeal that there is no evidence to support a finding of abuse of process.

propositions.text: The application judge asked the wrong question and applied the wrong test for abuse of process but did inquire into relevant considerations.
propositions.quote: While the application judge asked the wrong question and applied the wrong test for abuse of process, he did inquire into the considerations that informed the decision to repudiate, the process adopted, and the conduct of all Crown actors who were involved.

propositions.text: The application judge found no evidence of political interference or bad faith in the ADM's repudiation decision.
propositions.quote: he concluded that “there is absolutely no evidence” of political interference (para. 22) and “nothing to suggest that [the ADM’s] action was taken in bad faith or to accommodate a real or perceived political stance of his Minister of Justice” (para. 25).

propositions.text: The ADM repudiated due to errors in Crown counsel's conclusions and public interest concerns given the seriousness of the offences.
propositions.quote: Those who influenced [the ADM’s] decision to repudiate the resolution agreement took exception to a pair of [Crown counsel’s] conclusions: first, that the analyses of the breath samples provided by Ms. Nixon would be inadmissible at trial and second, that the evidence of Ryan Galloway...was too remote...In view of those two mistakes, the Assistant Deputy Minister was persuaded that any agreement which permitted Ms. Nixon to escape Criminal Code convictions was contrary to the public interest...he concluded that to honour it would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with the Court of Appeal that no abuse of process evidence exists; the application judge erred but examined relevant factors.

propositions.text: The application judge erred by dismissing the ADM’s opinion requiring more than differing senior counsel views.
propositions.quote: The application judge erred by summarily dismissing the ADM’s considered opinion on the ground that the Crown had to show more than “establish that other, even more senior counsel, have reached a different conclusion” than Crown counsel did (para. 27).

propositions.text: The application judge adopted Hill J.'s reasoning in R. v. M. (R.) that repudiation is not core prosecutorial discretion.
propositions.quote: On this point, the application judge adopted the reasoning of Hill J. in R. v. M. (R.) (2006), 83 O.R. (3d) 349 (S.C.J.). However, the approach adopted in M. (R.) is based on the erroneous view that “the act of repudiation is not an exercise of core prosecutorial discretion” (M. (R.), at para. 65 (emphasis in original)).

propositions.text: Hill J. viewed repudiation as governed by court's inherent jurisdiction, not prosecutorial discretion abuse of process.
propositions.quote: Hill J. was thus of the view that, while the plea agreement is not reviewable subject only to abuse of process, the repudiation is governed by the inherent jurisdiction of the court to control its own process (para. 62).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the application judge erred adopting Hill J.'s view that repudiation is not prosecutorial discretion but court process control.

propositions.text: The ADM’s repudiation decision falls within prosecutorial discretion and absent misconduct, is the Crown’s alone to make.
propositions.quote: As discussed earlier, the ADM’s decision to resile from the plea agreement falls within the scope of prosecutorial discretion. In the absence of any prosecutorial misconduct, improper motive or bad faith...the decision to proceed with the prosecution is the Crown’s alone to make.

propositions.text: Reasonable counsel may differ on public interest; ADM acted in good faith correcting errors and considering offence seriousness.
propositions.quote: Reasonable counsel may indeed, and often do, differ on whether a particular disposition is in the public interest...The ADM, in good faith, determined that Crown counsel’s assessment...was erroneous and...concluded that it would not be in the public interest to terminate the prosecution.

propositions.text: ADM’s decision cannot be regarded as misconduct.
propositions.quote: This can hardly be regarded as evidence of misconduct.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the ADM’s repudiation is prosecutorial discretion exercised in good faith without misconduct.

propositions.text: Plea agreements cannot be overturned arbitrarily; the decision method may reveal misconduct amounting to abuse of process.
propositions.quote: This does not mean that plea agreements can be overturned on a whim. The method by which the decision was reached can itself reveal misconduct of a sufficient degree to amount to abuse of process.

propositions.text: Repudiation here was rare, with only two prior Alberta occurrences, and no abusive conduct evidence in the process.
propositions.quote: The act of repudiation was indeed a rare and exceptional occurrence. The evidence revealed that there have been only two prior occurrences in Alberta...There was also no evidence of abusive conduct in the process leading to the decision to repudiate.

propositions.text: Paperny J.A. found the ADM acted fairly, reasonably, and expeditiously without prejudice or abuse of process.
propositions.quote: The ADM carefully reviewed the evidence...Having satisfied himself...he acted expeditiously...He also considered possible prejudice...The ADM’s conduct...cannot be characterized as unfair, unreasonable, oppressive or irrational. The high threshold to find abuse of process has not been met here.

paragraphs.summary: The court states plea repudiation here was rare, fair, and not abusive, agreeing with Paperny J.A.'s analysis.

propositions.text: Ms. Nixon was restored to her position before the plea agreement; no prejudice resulted from repudiation.
propositions.quote: Finally, Ms. Nixon was returned to the position she was in at the conclusion of the preliminary hearing before the plea agreement was entered into. There is no merit to the contention that she suffered prejudice as a result of the repudiation.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Ms. Nixon suffered no prejudice from the plea agreement repudiation.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, the appeal is dismissed. Appeal dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal.
